content: The estimation of HIV incidence, the number of people living with HIV, and the proportion of undiagnosed cases can be achieved using back-calculation methods. These methods rely on data from HIV/AIDS diagnoses and CD4 counts at the time of diagnosis. Such data are valuable for program planning when combined with national-level information derived from modeling tools like Spectrum AIM. The use of HIV case reporting data for surveillance is outlined in the UNAIDS/WHO guidelines for second-generation HIV surveillance, particularly in Module 1 (focused on understanding the epidemic) and Module 7 (focused on evaluating national surveillance systems). A dedicated module for HIV case reporting (Module 4: Surveillance of HIV infection using HIV case notification) is forthcoming. Outreach data are collected by NGOs and community health or outreach workers, who may or may not be affiliated with healthcare facilities. Depending on local policies and practices, NGOs may provide HIV testing, peer education, support, and critical follow-up care for the populations they serve. Their records offer essential insights into the connection between health facilities and communities. NGO outreach registers often include data on key populations, the reach of HIV prevention services, and referrals for HIV testing and treatment follow-up. These records can also help estimate the size of key population groups and contribute to sampling frames for surveys assessing treatment coverage and outcomes among these populations. Community health and outreach workers maintain records on the number of people in the community receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART), pregnant women, HIV-exposed infants, and their mothers. A formal data management link should be established between health facilities, NGO outreach programs, and communities in a given area. This arrangement should address recording, reporting, and referral procedures while ensuring confidentiality both within and outside health facilities. The completeness and quality of community data depend on the monitoring and evaluation (M&E) capacity of NGOs and community health workers. Identifying gaps in outreach capacity is crucial for determining the training needs of NGO staff and outreach workers. Community data collected by NGOs should be reported and integrated into central reporting systems, provided confidentiality is maintained. NGOs often play a critical role in reaching key populations, many of whom engage in stigmatized or illegal activities. Maintaining the anonymity of key population data is essential while ensuring adequate follow-up and continuity of care. Surveillance of the HIV/AIDS epidemic requires a comprehensive approach, as outlined in various UNAIDS and WHO guidelines. Administrative data systems at the facility level are used to support the smooth operation of health facilities and provide critical information for management regarding reach, coverage, and quality. These systems include lists of health facilities, records of human resources, and information on supplies and commodities. The data collected are typically counts of services provided or supplies consumed, rather than patient-specific care data. Supervisory visits and quality assessments can provide complementary information. Aggregating data from different health facilities is necessary for constructing indicators at national or subnational levels. However, variations in administrative systems across facilities can make data pooling challenging. Administrative data can also highlight system functionality issues, such as stock-outs of essential supplies, which can disrupt treatment and affect care quality. Monitoring stock management can identify gaps in procurement and distribution and suggest ways to prevent future stock-outs. Some strategic information systems generate dashboards to display early warning indicators, alerting program managers before stock-outs occur. Health expenditure data are collected to inform national policies and for international reporting. Understanding the flow of funds—from sources to decision-makers, providers, and ultimately to care recipients—is essential. Expenditure data can describe what has been purchased (e.g., salaries, commodities) and for what purpose (e.g., preventive or curative care). Two international systems, the National AIDS Spending Assessments (NASA) and Health Accounts (HA), track health spending by function, beneficiary, and funding source. These systems provide detailed information on HIV/AIDS and overall health spending, enabling evidence-based policymaking. NASA tracks financial flows and expenditures using globally standardized categories, providing indicators of a country’s financial response to AIDS. It supports monitoring resource mobilization and compliance with donor requirements. While not an accounting system, NASA tracks spending as reported by countries. Health Accounts, on the other hand, track all health spending in a country over a defined period, generating consistent and comprehensive data for policy-making. They are conducted annually and can monitor changes in resource allocation and expenditure resulting from policy reforms or new programs. Household surveys, such as the Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) and AIDS Indicator Survey (AIS), often include HIV testing and collect data on risk behaviors, service utilization, and attitudes toward HIV-related stigma. These surveys provide a snapshot of HIV-related indicators in a representative sample of the population and are typically conducted every five years. When repeated over time, they allow for trend analysis to monitor progress toward national and global goals. However, household surveys are not recommended in countries with concentrated or low-level epidemics due to their limited ability to reach key populations and the large sample sizes required for representative data. Surveys targeting key populations at higher risk for HIV, such as sex workers, people who inject drugs, and men who have sex with men, are essential for obtaining representative data on their seroprevalence, risk behaviors, and service utilization. Integrated Bio-Behavioral Surveys (IBBS) are particularly important in national strategies focusing on key populations. Even in generalized epidemics, key populations can significantly contribute to the HIV burden due to their higher prevalence and incidence rates. IBBS data provide critical information on disease burden and treatment needs.
